title: Set the tube GRADE from the shock case — and stop arguing about wall thickness

ideaData.title: Set the tube GRADE from the shock case — and stop arguing about wall thickness
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): The tube is not sized by wall thickness, it is sized by grade. At the 4,670 Nm* rear design case the shear stress is 286 MPa (tau = T x r_outer / J), which needs a yield strength near 500 MPa just to stay elastic under von Mises. Torsional buckling has a margin of about 2.5 by the Donnell relation, so buckling is not the constraint. Dana state that high-strength steel tubing gives maximum torque capacity at minimum practical weight — this card puts a number on what 'high-strength' has to mean here. SPEC: tube grade specified at Re >= 500 MPa (E470 / S500MC class) and stated on the drawing; shear stress 286 MPa at the 4,670 Nm* PROPSHAFT design case, 235 MPa at the 3,839 Nm* steady case; wall HELD at 2.0 mm
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): +£0.90* over a mild grade. SPEC: tube grade specified at Re >= 500 MPa (E470 / S500MC class) and stated on the drawing; shear stress 286 MPa at the 4,670 Nm* PROPSHAFT design case, 235 MPa at the 3,839 Nm* steady case; wall HELD at 2.0 mm
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: None on duty, but it removes a latent one. A mild tube would yield at the shock case. Trade-off: Proven · effort Low. Trade: THIS CARD REPLACES THE THINNER-WALL IDEA AND KILLS IT. Taking the wall to 1.8 mm raises the required yield to about 547 MPa AND drops the buckling margin from 2.5 to 1.95 — both criteria move the wrong way, for about a pound. Sheet 1 block H2 shows the arithmetic.

title: Greasable Cardan joints with a centrally located grease fitting

ideaData.title: Greasable Cardan joints with a centrally located grease fitting

ideaData.title: Specify flat-ended needle rollers with thrust washers

title: Tuned internal liner damper instead of relying on balance alone

ideaData.title: Tuned internal liner damper instead of relying on balance alone
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): Cardboard, foam and rubber liners are long-standing practice for attenuating BENDING mode vibration inside a propshaft tube. American Axle's patent literature is explicit that shell mode is a separate problem those liners do not solve, and that its tuned damper pairs a liner tuned to bending and torsion modes with a damping member aimed at shell mode, contacting the tube over no more than 5% of the liner's own contact area. It is also explicit that long aluminium propshafts produce significant shell-mode noise and are generally obliged to carry damping treatments — and that those treatments mass-load the tube and pull critical speed back down. SPEC: tuned liner fitted to the rear tube: liner mass and stiffness tuned to the first bending mode, damping member tuned to the measured shell-mode frequency; added mass held under 0.25 kg* so the whirl margin stays above 3.0x; damper-to-tube contact area under 5%*
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): +£2.60* — a cost ADDER. SPEC: tuned liner fitted to the rear tube: liner mass and stiffness tuned to the first bending mode, damping member tuned to the measured shell-mode frequency; added mass held under 0.25 kg* so the whirl margin stays above 3.0x; damper-to-tube contact area under 5%*
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: Re-validate. Order analysis at vehicle level, and the whirl gate re-run because any insert mass-loads the tube. Trade-off: Proven · effort Low. Trade: it is an adder and I am not proposing it for the steel baseline, which has 3.65x whirl margin and no known shell-mode complaint. It is here because it is the PRE-CONDITION for ideas D1 and D9 — any longer or thinner tube will need it, and the mass it adds has to be costed against the margin it eats.

title: Magnetic pulse weld the yokes to the tube instead of MIG welding

ideaData.title: Magnetic pulse weld the yokes to the tube instead of MIG welding
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): Dana's patent literature is direct about the mechanism: joints attached by conventional welding produce imbalance in the driveshaft, which is why the shaft then has to be balanced, and the balancing operation adds both cost and weight. Magnetic pulse welding is a solid-state process with negligible heating and no heat-affected zone, and it has been implemented specifically to improve driveshaft balance during manufacture, reducing the need for post-manufacture balancing. So the saving is not in the weld — it is downstream, in balance minutes and in the weights that no longer have to be applied. SPEC: yoke-to-tube joining changed to MPW; welding cut from 1.5 to 1.0 min per joint and rear balance from 9.0 to 7.0 min; concentricity to the tube held within 0.10 mm* and verified on 30 parts*; residual unbalance target set from the half-critical requirement, not from habit
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): -£3.98*. SPEC: yoke-to-tube joining changed to MPW; welding cut from 1.5 to 1.0 min per joint and rear balance from 9.0 to 7.0 min; concentricity to the tube held within 0.10 mm* and verified on 30 parts*; residual unbalance target set from the half-critical requirement, not from habit
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: Re-validate. Weld-zone behaviour changes completely — there is no HAZ — so the torsional durability block is re-run. Trade-off: EMERGING, not Proven · effort Medium. Trade: MATURITY IS THE ISSUE AND I WILL NOT OVERSTATE IT. Trade reporting has noted that no high-volume facility had put pulsed magnetic welding into serial production, and 2025 process research still reports scalability limits for large-diameter tubes. This is an RFQ question to Dana, not a commitment we make.

title: One-piece ALUMINIUM rear propshaft, deleting the centre bearing

ideaData.title: One-piece ALUMINIUM rear propshaft, deleting the centre bearing
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): A larger-diameter aluminium tube at the same mass raises critical speed enough to span the whole distance in one piece, deleting the centre bearing, one Cardan joint and one weld yoke. Magnetic pulse welding is the enabling process for the aluminium-tube-to-steel-yoke joint, because it is solid state and suited to dissimilar metals. SPEC: ALTERNATIVE to D9 — both delete the SAME three parts, so at most one can be captured; rear shaft becomes a single 100 x 3.0 mm aluminium tube over 1,450 mm; critical speed 7,776 rpm, a 1.84x margin over 4,226 rpm, half-critical at 166 km/h; one-piece STEEL at the same length is ruled out at 5,943 rpm with a 127 km/h half-critical
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): -£23.90* and about -3.5 kg* — ALTERNATIVE TO D9, NOT ADDITIONAL. SPEC: ALTERNATIVE to D9 — both delete the SAME three parts, so at most one can be captured; rear shaft becomes a single 100 x 3.0 mm aluminium tube over 1,450 mm; critical speed 7,776 rpm, a 1.84x margin over 4,226 rpm, half-critical at 166 km/h; one-piece STEEL at the same length is ruled out at 5,943 rpm with a 127 km/h half-critical
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: Re-validate everything. Larger droop angles with no intermediate support, and second order grows with the SQUARE of the angle. Trade-off: Proven on road cars · effort High. Trade: I AM NOW RECOMMENDING AGAINST THIS, ON EVIDENCE RATHER THAN INSTINCT, AND IDEA D9 SUPERSEDES IT. Three sourced objections. First, long aluminium propshafts are documented as producing significant shell-mode noise and being generally obliged to carry damping treatments — and those treatments mass-load the tube, so the 1.84x margin is optimistic before damping is fitted. Second, aluminium is notch sensitive, and magnetic-pulse-FORMED tube-to-yoke joints have a documented history of slippage under torque producing a loud noise, with fatigue life falling as torque rises; our design case is 4,670 Nm, which is high. Third, an aluminium tube dents under rock strike where a steel one recovers, and the shaft is the lowest rotating part under this vehicle.

SPEC: ALTERNATIVE to D1 — both delete the SAME centre bearing, Cardan joint and weld yoke, so at most one can be captured; rear propshaft shortened by at least 120 mm* by flange-mounting the transfer case to the gearbox; one-piece STEEL at 1,330 mm then reaches 7,064 rpm critical, a 1.67x margin over 4,226 rpm and a half-critical road speed of 150 km/h, clear of the 80-113 km/h band; deletes the centre bearing, 1 Cardan joint and 1 weld yoke

ideaData.studyCombinedCapture: COMBINED CAPTURE — honest, and NOT the sum. The saving cards add to roughly £80, and that number is wrong for five reasons. D9 is £35.68 of it and D1 is a further £23.90 — but they are ALTERNATIVES, not additions: both delete the same centre bearing, the same Cardan joint and the same weld yoke, so at most one of them can ever be captured. D9 is the better of the two and it is not a propshaft decision at all; it needs the transfer case flange-mounted at the concept gate. D5 needs the flange interfaces made common, which is a transfer case and axle decision. P1, P2 and P3 are all things the SUPPLIER does, so we capture them through the RFQ rather than in our own plant — and P1's maturity is Emerging, not Proven. And M1 has stopped being a saving at all: the tube grade is set by the shock case, so it is now a £0.90 adder that removes a latent failure. A realistic engineering-only capture, excluding D1 and D9, is £12-14* gross; net of the M1, M3, M4 and M5 adders it is £6-12* on a £208 assembly, roughly 3-6%. Add the RFQ at -12% and it becomes £31-37*. If the concept gate clears D9 — and it is worth a further £15.56 in the transfer-case study for the same package change — the total reaches £67-73*. THAT is the number to commit to, and note what changed: the best idea in this study is not a propshaft idea, and it only exists because the whirl arithmetic was written down.

ideaData.reviewOpenPoints: [MAJOR · consistency] There is a cross-study contradiction on the shortening. PS26 D9 needs 'at least 120 mm' of rear-shaft shortening from flange-mounting the transfer case, and calls it the same package change as TC26 D3. TC26 D3 says that change shortens the driveline by about 35 mm. The required length is also not set by the workbook's own gate: its table already rates 1,400 mm (-50 mm) as 'OK', and 1,450 mm (no shortening) as only 'MARGINAL'. So '120 mm minimum' is not a gate requirement. Evidence: PS register D9: 'rear propshaft shortened by at least 120 mm* by flange-mounting the transfer case'; TC register D3: 'overall driveline length shortened by about 35 mm*'; PS sheet 1 rows 92/124: '1.45 m ... 1.41x ... 126.6 km/h ... MARGINAL'; '1400 ... 1.51x ... 135.8 km/h ... OK — one-piece STEEL is available at this length' Recommendation: Ask the author to reconcile 35 mm against 120 mm, and to state the shortening the gate actually needs. The £35.68 saving depends on that package change being achievable. ¶ [MINOR · consistency] PS26 says the transfer-case study is worth 'a further £15.56'. The TC26 register gives -£16 for D3. It is a rounding difference: €18 × 0.8644 = £15.56. But £15.56 is also PS26 D3's own adder figure, which invites confusion. Evidence: PS combined capture: 'worth a further £15.56 in the transfer-case study'; TC D3 '-£16*' Recommendation: Quote the TC figure as written (-£16), or state 'TC D3 €18 = £15.56'. ¶ [MINOR · quality] The card shows £2.85M/yr. It is a mutually exclusive alternative to D1 (which shows £1.91M), and it needs a transfer-case package change at the concept gate. The volumeBasis note says this generically, but nothing on the card itself does. Evidence: Cost effect: '-£35.68* ... ALTERNATIVE TO D1, NOT ADDITIONAL' Recommendation: Fine as long as the cost-effect text is visible on the card. Add a 'mutually exclusive with ps26-d1' tag.

description: [Prop-Shaft Study 2026 · Saving] Shorten the rear shaft instead of changing its material — flange-mount the transfer case. Critical speed scales as 1/L^2, so LENGTH is a far stronger lever than material, and Dana say the same thing from the other direction: increased tube diameter allows a higher critical speed and longer one-piece driveshafts. Mercedes already do this in production — the G-Class W464 transfer case is flange-mounted directly onto the 9G-TRONIC, which shortens the rear propshaft for nothing. Shorten our shaft enough and a ONE-PIECE STEEL shaft clears the half-critical band that rules it out today, delivering exactly the same deletions as D1 with none of aluminium's problems.
